title: Physics-constrained machine learning for decoding multi-nanobubble configurations in graphene
authors: Jihye Kim, Taegeun Song, Nojoon Myoung
abstract: Identifying multiple graphene nanobubbles from electronic spectra is challenging because their strain-induced features overlap. We develop a physics-constrained machine-learning framework that decodes nanobubble configurations from density-of-states (DOS) spectra. For spatially separated nanobubbles, previous full quantum-transport calculations established that the multi-bubble DOS is numerically equivalent to the normalized sum of the constituent single-bubble spectra. We encode this validated additive relation in a compact neural decomposition model. For each target spectrum, the basis coefficients are optimized independently, and the resulting weights directly identify the constituent geometries. The method accurately reconstructs configurations of increasing complexity and remains robust to repeated constituents, incomplete basis dictionaries, and simulated measurement noise. The framework provides an interpretable route for characterizing strain-engineered graphene nanostructures and may extend to other quantum materials with additive spectral responses.
summary: The paper presents a novel, physics-constrained machine learning method to decode the arrangement of multiple nanobubbles in graphene by analyzing their composite electronic Density-of-States spectra. It exploits the known additive relationship between single and multi-bubble DOS signatures to decompose the measured spectrum into constituent geometries. This provides an interpretable tool for characterizing strain-engineered quantum materials.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately identifying multiple, overlapping nanobubble configurations within graphene solely from their composite electronic Density-of-States (DOS) spectra.
main_result: The developed framework successfully reconstructs complex bubble arrangements with high fidelity and robustness against noise and missing basis components by leveraging a physics-constrained decomposition model.
method: A physics-constrained machine learning approach is used to decompose the measured composite DOS spectrum into a sum of known single-bubble spectra, treating it as an inverse problem solved via neural network optimization.
model_or_system: The system is graphene containing multiple nanobubbles, modeled using tight-binding Hamiltonian calculations. The core physical constraint exploited is that the multi-bubble DOS is additively equivalent to the sum of its constituent single-bubble spectra for separated bubbles.
key_observables: Optimized basis coefficients (weights) which directly identify the geometry and multiplicity of each constituent nanobubble; composition error quantified by normalized L1 weight deviation ($\delta w$).
important_parameters: The number of nanobubbles ($N$), the degree of spectral overlap, and the level of added Gaussian white noise ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The method fundamentally relies on the validated additive relationship between the multi-bubble DOS and the sum of single-bubble spectra, which is assumed to hold for sufficiently separated bubbles.
figures_summary: Figures demonstrate reconstruction fidelity for increasing bubble complexity (up to ten) and test robustness by showing successful decomposition when constituents are repeated or when the basis dictionary is incomplete. Noise tests quantify performance degradation as a function of added noise amplitude.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem (overlapping DOS), introduces the physics-constrained ML framework based on the additive spectral relation, details the methodology using neural decomposition in log space, and validates its robustness through systematic testing against noise and incomplete basis sets.
why_interesting: This work exemplifies applying advanced machine learning techniques to solve complex inverse problems in condensed matter spectroscopy. The use of physical constraints (the additive DOS rule) within a differentiable ML framework is highly relevant for interpreting spectroscopic data from quantum materials.

The left panel illustrates a graphene nanoribbon containing multiple nanobubbles, each characterized by its height h and lateral width σ. The middle panel shows the dataset-generation procedure: single-bubble DOS basis spectra are obtained from quantum-transport simulations using the Kwant Python package and are com- bined as a normalized sum to construct composite multi-nanobubble spectra. This construction follows the previously verified numerical equivalence between full multi-bubble calculations and summed single-bubble spectra for sufficiently separated...

Figure 2: Reconstruction of composite DOS spectra for multi-nanobubble configurations. The original composite spectra (black) are compared with spectra reconstructed through spectrum- specific coefficient optimization (red) for systems containing (a) one, (b) five, and (c) ten nanobubbles. The insets show the corresponding optimized weight distributions over the single- bubble basis library. The close agreement between the curves indicates that the decomposition identifies and reconstructs the constituent contributions as the number of nanobubbles increases.

Figure 3: Tests beyond idealized basis conditions. (a) Reconstruction of an imbalanced configuration containing two identical nanobubbles and one distinct nanobubble, showing that the decomposition identifies repeated basis components through their fractional multiplicity weights. (b) Reconstruction with an incomplete basis dictionary, in which one of the three constituent nanobubbles is absent from the available dictionary; the number of basis channels is reduced from 76 to 70. In both panels, the original DOS is shown in black, the reconstructed DOS is shown in red, and the insets display the optimized basis weights.

Figure 4: Robustness against additive Gaussian white noise in the log-transformed input spectra. Top: representative noisy log-DOS spectra obtained by adding Gaussian white noise after logarithmic transformation; the noisy inputs are shown in red. Bottom: mean normalized L1 weight error δw as a function of the mean noise amplitude for configurations containing N = 1, 3, and 5 nanobubbles. At each noise level, the averages are taken over 7, 6, and 8 independent realizations for N = 1, 3, and 5, respectively; the vertical error bars denote the standard deviation of δw.
